brief.situation: 09:00 in an outpatient orthopedic clinic (direct access). You are the physical therapist. Jordan, 27, rolled his right ankle inward in a basketball game last night and hopped off the court. He wants to 'get moving' and play Saturday.
handover: He has not seen a physician or had imaging.

Clinic policy: a positive Ottawa ankle rule screen is sent for radiographs the same day through the clinic's referring physician before loading; functional rehabilitation starts once fracture is excluded.

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: An inversion injury loads the anterior talofibular ligament, but tenderness at the posterior lateral malleolus and inability to bear weight four steps make the Ottawa rules positive: a fracture must be excluded first.
parts.modelAnswer: It's an inversion sprain mechanism, but he's tender on the back edge of the lateral malleolus and can't take four steps, so Ottawa says X-ray before anything else.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Protected weight bearing and same-day radiographs; if no fracture, early functional rehab with progressive balance training instead of prolonged immobilization; no drills now.
parts.modelAnswer: Crutches and X-rays today. If it's clear, early functional rehab and balance work, not weeks in a boot. No drills now.

scoring.modelReasoning: Inversion injuries load the anterior talofibular ligament, and syndesmotic (high ankle) sprains carry more morbidity. Before treating a sprain, apply the Ottawa ankle rules: bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of a malleolus, or inability to bear weight four steps, means radiographs. Jordan's screen is positive, so protect the ankle and image the same day. If there is no fracture, early functional mobilization beats prolonged rest, and a neuromuscular and balance program reduces recurrence.
